In the analysis of blends that consist of multiple substances, it's common to assess the average composition of these blends. This task involves estimating the parameters of a mixture model, which can be achieved through maximum likelihood estimation. However, evaluating the average parameter of blends is a more complex problem that requires careful consideration of several factors, including the presence of invisible components, model misspecification, and the effects of sampling and measurement errors. This study develops a method for assessing the average parameter of blends based on general models, provides corrections for visible component weights, and introduces weighted versions of the Wald and likelihood ratio tests to evaluate model validity. Additionally, we discuss the assessment of average parameters for hidden components, the calculation of confidence intervals, and the evaluation of uncertainty in the average parameter of blends. This research builds upon previous work by modifying the formulas for hidden component weights and weighted tests, and offers practical applications to the analysis of blending data, including quality control and regulatory purposes. This study's methods are illustrated through numerical examples and real-world data sets. This research also explores the relationship between the method of assessment and other approaches to mixture model analysis, including the isobestic method, the weighted mean, and maximum likelihood estimation. This example highlights that the property of density among distributional operators does not extend to non-compact settings. Creating effective proof systems for SMT solvers involves a delicate balance in designing a format that is both convenient for users and soluble for verifiers. A perfect format would be both easy to formulate and efficient for validation. Prior evidence frameworks fall into one of two categories: formats that facilitate user creativity but are difficult for verifiers to validate, or those that are simple to validate but restrictive for users. We propose "Universal SMT Evidence" (USE), a format that combines the convenience of a procedural proof system with the simplicity of a direct formulation, allowing user flexibility while ensuring solvers can easily validate the format. We have implemented USE in Alethe, a verification tool for SMT proofs that supports multiple solvers, including Z3, CVC4, and VeriT. Proofs formulated using USE can be validated on a broad scale, across various solvers and theories. We have conducted experiments demonstrating that a significant portion of existing benchmark proofs are susceptible to solvers that were unknown at the time of our investigation. Additionally, we have discovered that verifiable formulations tend to be more efficient than non-verifiable formulations, reducing the size of proofs by an average of 20%. Lastly, we have found that a subset of user-interactive theories, such as floating-point arithmetic, could significantly benefit from a proof validation process, given the frequent occurrence of assertions against these theories. We have made Alethe available to the public via an open-source license, inviting contributions and feedback from the community. Moreover, we have incorporated USE support into the SMT-L3 standard, a proposal that is currently under review. We hope that this proof format, along with Alethe, will contribute to more reliable and efficient verification tasks, and we welcome further collaboration on our initiatives. We have presented two versions of the paper, one for the Formal Methods: Foundations and Applications conference and a longer version available via arXiv. We have also demonstrated that a more restrictive version of USE, which we call Simple SMT Evidence (SSE), is sufficiently expressive to capture the core concepts of existing evidence formats, including the CVC4 proof system, Z3's Solitaire, and VeriT's Jeli wrapper, as well as a proposed format called ProofSpec. We believe that SSE provides a unified perspective on these formats and proves the existence of a single, unified evidence format that is capable of capturing the diversity of SMT solvers and theories. This paper introduces two significant innovations in federated learning with synchronous aggregation. Firstly, we relax the assumption that participants have access to high-quality gradients, now requiring only the use of unconstrained gradient updates. Secondly, we enhance the efficiency of training by allowing participants to submit updates that have been computed in advance, without the need to wait for the next scheduling interval. We derive a new learning rate schedule and establish upper bounds on the time it takes for the algorithm to converge, also finding that the convergence rate can be improved by increasing the scheduling interval. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of our approach by conducting experiments on real datasets,, and show that our method exceeds the performance of baseline methods,, and that the benefits of our approach increase in proportion to the difficulty of the dataset. We have open-sourced our code for public use.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across languages with different character sets. In this paper, we introduce a new ASR transfer approach, incorporating a two-step process where a coarse neural recognizer is employed to provide a more manageable amount of text data by transcribing rough outputs, and this is followed by fine-tuning a separate neural model to achieve more precise transcription. We successfully applied this method to transfer ASR systems between Chinese and Korean languages. Our experiments revealed this transfer method is effective in both within-language and cross-language settings, outperforming existing approaches by 8% in within-language experiments and demonstrating the feasibility of transferring ASR systems between Chinese and Korean languages with only 0.7 million training data. Our findings also showed that this method can be suitable for low-resource languages by reducing the word error rate from 21.4% to 13.6% in Korean. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChengxiangGo/R2DTF_framework.

The task of allocating precious goods to self-interested individuals in an environment of competition can be a complex challenge. This issue arises frequently in real-world scenarios, such as dividing spectrum licenses among mobile operators, allocating time slots for satellite transmissions, or distributing wealth among powerful agents. These situations share a common characteristic: the individuals involved seek to maximize their own gains and are capable of manipulating their behavior to achieve more equitable outcomes. In addition, a fair and stable allocation must be able to withstand attempts by these self-interested individuals to manipulate the process, a property known as purity, as well as resistance to reverse, a property known as submularity. Furthermore, the allocation should be equitable, a property known as proportionality. In our research, we demonstrate the existence of pure Nash equilibria in a wide range of scenarios, as well as identifying specific instances where such equilibria are remarkably proportional. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to the presence of opposing actions, such as cooperation and competition, without clear distinction. Current offline learning methods fail to utilize informative negative trajectory data, which holds significant value, given that it demonstrates the boundaries of which actions are not desirable. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called Positive Trajectory Learning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (PTMARL). This approach leverages negative trajectory data by framing the problem within a comparison learning framework, effectively enabling the comparison of action trajectories. We evaluate our approach on various offline datasets and encounter notable performance gains, particularly when considering sparse reward signals. Our results le us to believe that comparing action trajectories with a proper comparison loss can lead to more efficient learning. We make all source code and datasets available at GitHub: https://github.com/lingyu-gh/PTMARL.

By analyzing various preparations of the single particle, we showed that nonlocality and entanglement are equivalent properties that can be measured in the same way. Our findings also highlight that single-particle nonlocality is resistant to the action of decoherence, which is caused by interactions with the surrounding environment. The interplay of interactions and frustration in correlated systems, which often rely on nuclear momentum, presents a significant obstacle in achieving with lattice displacement-driven spectroscopies like stop-flow and freeze-drying techniques. Despite this challenge, achieving this goal is crucial for understanding interactions, identifying emergent orders, and determining the localization of electrons. We introduce nuclear phase recovery spectroscopy, a technique that expands on resonant x-ray scattering by incorporating phase information from x-ray fluctuations. This method allows for the direct determination of nuclear phases, even in isolated crystals, and enables the study of dynamics and interactions in condensed matter systems. As an example, we apply this technique to freeze-dried, stop-flow DNA-tethered gold nanoparticles, demonstrating its capability in describing the phase evolution of a single component. However, this technique's true potential is revealed when we extend it to complex systems, such as DNA-tethered nanoparticles in tethers, demonstrating the capability to extract rich information about dynamics, interactions, and initial conditions. This technique is versatile and can be implemented using standard x-ray scattering equipment, making it suitable for a wide range of materials and biological systems. Moreover, it offers a feasible approach to stop-flow and freeze-drying geometries, allowing for the recovery of phases from 2D scattering patterns along with the development of theoretical tools to characterize initial conditions, interactions, and dynamics in space and time. Lastly, this approach provides a means of investigating order parameters in chemical reactions, offering insights into the localization of electrons and the onset of orders in low-dimensional systems. We propose this technique be referred to as nuclear phase recovery spectroscopy. This research introduces a novel numerical method to model single-phase Darcy flow within porous media containing fractures. Based on finite element fundamentals, the technique combines two main methods to model flow: finite difference methods for describing flow within fracture channels and finite element methods for modeling flow within solid media. The approach involves converting finite difference methods into a form that can be integrated with finite element algorithms. This is achieved by utilizing the precise values of fracture channel flow velocities at nodal points, rather than calculating approximate values of flow rates at grid points as is common in finite difference methods. This technique has been applied to several test cases, including complex scenarios with moving water fronts, compared against established reference solutions. The results show that this method delivers highly accurate and stable numerical data, and can be efficiently applied to real-world problems of single-phase flow within fractured media. The code developed as part of this research can be used as a starting point for further developments, such as incorporating nonlinear flow models, time-dependent flow scenarios, and two-phase flow scenarios. The code is written in the MATLAB programming language. The technique and code presented here offer a hybrid alternative to existing combined numerical methods, specifically the conventional finite difference-finite element technique, and can be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working with flow simulations in fractured media. The code is available for public use upon requesting access from the author. The technique and code developed also form the basis for further research into combined numerical methods, specifically the integration of finite element algorithms with other point-based flow solvers. The code has been tested using three increasingly complex test cases, including a scenario with moving water fronts, and produces highly accurate and stable numerical results compared to established reference solutions. Hypothesis testing based on Bayesian methods uses Bayes factors, which quantify the ratio of model probabilities with and without the tested hypothesis. Although the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCCM) method is commonly used to compute Bayes factors, its implementation is often challenging due to its high computational requirements and sensitivity to the number of Monte Carlo chains. Alternatively, the bridge sampling method is proposed to determine Bayes factors in a more efficient manner. However, the optimal way to implement this method on a Monte Carlo sample is less clear and needs further investigation. This study examines the accuracy and efficiency of three Monte Carlo workflow strategies for computing Bayes factors using bridge sampling. The results show that two variants of the posterior ratio strategy achieve highly accurate results, with the optimal choice depending on the specificity of the current Monte Carlo sample. Additionally, the study finds that the marginal likelihood strategy is less precise and considers the accuracy of this method's marginal likelihood estimates as critical to its performance. Moreover, the study examines the factors that influence the accuracy of the marginal likelihood estimates and presents a set of best practices for implementing the bridge sampling method, including using multiple Monte Carlo samples and evaluating the accuracy of the marginal likelihood estimates using the Bayes factor uncertainty criterion. This study is applicable to a broad range of statistical models and provides a general framework for evaluating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates based on Monte Carlo samples. This research also addresses the issue of Bayes factor estimate uncertainty in the context of the Bayesian hypothesis testing framework and considers the recent proposal of a new performance criterion that takes into account the uncertainty of the Bayes factor estimates. This criterion is more reliable than the commonly used criterion based on the standard error of the Bayes factor estimates and can be evaluated using the Monte Carlo workflow strategies developed in this study. This research further examines the relationship between the number of Monte Carlo samples and the accuracy of the Bayes factor estimates and finds that the accuracy of the estimates improves at a decreasing rate with the increase in the number of samples. This study also explores the recent proposal of a new performance criterion for Bayes factor estimates and finds that the accuracy of the estimates is characterized by a power law, which implies that the majority of the Bayes factor estimates are concentrated at the edges of the probability interval. In written communication between humans and AI, certain discourse markers such as "however" and "nevertheless" convey similar meanings, yet their implications vary. For example, some like "however" may imply a contradiction, whereas others like "in addition" indicate inclusion. To evaluate the intricate world of discourse indicators, researchers and developers rely on manual techniques, but with the growing complexity of language models, a systematic approach is necessary to keep up with the task. To address this challenge, we present a method for categorizing and analyzing discourse indicators, which can be applied to evaluate language models' performance, specifically in the context of contrastive dialogue. To validate our approach, we tested it on contrastive dialogue and found that it can distinguish between indicators that express contrast and those that do not. Furthermore, we incorporated it into a previous strategy for predicting the discourse indicators used by human interlocutors, and with it, we were able to incorporate features related to categorization, which enabled a 10% improvement in accuracy. Our method, discsense, is a flexible tool that allows for the exploration of various features and algorithms, and we have made it available online for others to use. In the context of human-language contrastive dialogue, our results indicate that the most effective features relate to the content and structure of the discourse, and we have discussed their implications. Finally, we concluded by discussing potential directions for future work, including the integration of discsense with existing frameworks for evaluating the coherence of human-language dialogue. Our code has been uploaded to github.com/ghraesh/ DiscSense.

Neural networks used in sensitive applications like facial recognition must ensure the trustworthiness of their results. Yet, without proper protection, these networks are vulnerable to being compromised by malicious attackers who could influence the data used for training, or by hardware failures that could affect accuracy. In response to these challenges, researchers are developing methods to validate the validity of neural network outputs, including checking the class probability and verifying that hardware errors are within safe limits. For networks like CNNs, which are known for their high efficiency and accuracy, researchers have several validation approaches available, including monitoring the range of activations, but none of these methods have been formally proven to guarantee the reliability of CNNs in the presence of hardware failures that cause temporary, precise changes to activations. This paper fills this gap by providing a formal proof that a specific, simple method called Activation Range Monitoring, which involves monitoring the range of activations and checking the class probability, guarantees the reliability of CNNs in the presence of hardware failures that cause temporary, precise changes to activations. This proof assumes an approach called robust classification, where a sample belongs to a class if the majority of neural network outputs for that sample indicate that class, and it also assumes that the range of activations is known and remains within a specific, known range. This proof is important because it provides a formal basis for a method that is already being used in practice, and it offers a starting point for further research into the development of reliable neural networks. This paper also includes a discussion about the limitations of the current method and the challenges of developing a more general approach to validate the validity of neural network outputs. This discussion includes a way to expand the current method to validate the validity of neural networks used in classification applications, and it also includes a way to develop a more general approach that does not rely on the assumption that the range of activations is known and remains within a specific, known range. This paper concludes by outlining the main results and presenting some related work in the area of facial recognition. Our approach creates a unified framework for translating between multiple languages by organizing words into shared semantic clusters, which share equivalent structures across different languages. To accomplish this, we develop a novel method that generates multilingual word representations, ensuring clusters are linguistically neutral and consistent across languages. Our approach utilizes a novel cluster-consistent objective function, combining clustering and translation tasks, to achieve this level of neutrality. We implemented this method using multi-task learning, latent representation, and clustering techniques and created a model for 14 languages, including English, Spanish, French, and Hindi. Our evaluation showed that the model outperforms current multilingual models in multiple metrics, surpassing the state-of-the-art in low-resource language translation tasks. Moreover, our analysis discovered that the proportion of shared clusters to unique clusters in each language directly correlates with translation difficulty, as measured by the age and complexity of the language. Notably, our approach also enhances monolingual embedding quality, as demonstrated by the improvement in evaluation metrics such as Multilingual Word Embedding Evaluation and Semantic Clustering Performance. To facilitate widespread use, we made the pre-trained model available publicly. Our code has been contributed to the open-source community under the FairSeq repository. Our proposed approach and resulting model prove that the notion of "one-size-fits-all" translation is feasible and efficient, achieving the best results to date in multiple evaluation metrics. Our analysis has far-reaching implications for natural language processing, suggesting that the difficulty of a language can be quantified based on the level of its linguistic structure, which may also apply to other tasks like summarization. To further validate this hypothesis, we developed a new ranking system for languages based on their proposed difficulty scores, employed it to conduct a rigorous analysis of various semantic clusters, and demonstrated that it accurately reflects the inherent challenges of each language. Moreover, this ranking system enabled us to prioritize the order in which languages should be integrated into a multilingual framework, leading to a significant improvement in performance when tested against a range of single-language and multilingual translation tasks. Our approach has numerous potential applications in real-world settings, across industries and platforms, which place a high value on scalable and efficient multilingual translation solutions. Moreover, this ranking system can be used across other natural language processing tasks like text classification, where the challenge of each language also correlates with its age and complexity. Unlike traditional regular expressions, REIs exclude the union operation and are instead characterized by inequalities of the form $x \subseteq y$, where $x$ and $y$ are regular expressions. Additionally, our method introduces a new concept known as the closure of a set of REIs, which can be determined in a polynomial time. We also establish a connection between REIs and regular expression satisfiability, demonstrating that determining whether a regular expression is satisfiable reduces to examining if a specific set of REIs is satisfiable. We also offer a concise overview of the basic principles underlying regular expression builder backwards approach, which is a key component of our solution, by introducing a simple symbolic language known as SBE. Recently, visual-inertial navigation methods have demonstrated high accuracy in navigating indoor environments, without the need for GPS, by combining visual and inertial sensors' data. While these methods show promise for indoor mobile robot applications, there's still room to improve their performance in complex scenarios, with extensive motion and light variations. To enhance the accuracy of these methods, researchers have employed recurrent models to incorporate past sensor data, but such approaches overwhelm the state estimation process with excessive temporal information, making it challenging to achieve a balance between the influence of current and past data. To address this issue, an external memory attention mechanism is proposed in this paper, allowing for a flexible balance between the impact of current and past data, while trimming the necessary temporal information to 10% of usual levels. With this proposed mechanism, a visual-inertial navigation framework is developed that utilizes the estimated state and the external memory to update the attention-weighted past information. By refining the state with respect to the weighted past information, the accuracy of the navigation is enhanced, while keeping the required temporal information minimal. The results show that this paper's method outperforms state-of-the-art visual-inertial navigation methods in complex scenarios with extensive motion and light variations, as demonstrated in extensive indoor simulations and real-world experiments. Furthermore, external memory attention enables efficient navigation in situations that require a long observation period, without the need for an increase in the prediction horizon, as shown in a comparison with regular recurrent-based methods. The proposed method's efficiency and accuracy also make it suitable for real-world applications on mobile robots, without the need for simulation-based hyperparameter tuning. This study addresses the numerical solution to the inverse problem of determining a source term in Maxwell's equations given output data. The solution approach proposed here is based on the quasi-reversibility method, which enables the formulation of an auxiliary problem closely related to the original problem but solvable using standard numerical methods. The auxiliary problem is formulated as a boundary value problem for a system of Maxwell's equations with a source term in the form of a Laplacian, which can be efficiently solved using finite element methods. The accuracy of the proposed method is evaluated through numerical experiments conducted using finite element methods and comparison with exact solutions. The results obtained indicate that the proposed method yields accurate solutions for different types of input data and confirms the impact of the method's stability factor on the solution's accuracy. We introduce the concept of discriminability duration, a measure that indicates the time it takes for two non-interacting quantum systems to differ significantly based on their combined state. This duration can be thought of as a variant of the coherence time, and its significance is demonstrated in the context of quantum communication, where it represents the time it takes for two separated systems to develop distinct characteristics. The rate at which this duration changes indicates the speed at which the systems' behavior varies, and this speed can be referred to as quantum velocity. We develop a general approach to analyze quantum velocity by examining how the discriminability duration changes as the orientation of one system's state changes. This change is represented by a variety of metrics, and we show that the most appropriate one is asymmetry, due to its straightforward relationship with the discriminability duration. As a result, we can determine the minimum possible change in asymmetry within a specific time period, which occurs when the two systems have orthogonal states. This minimum change indicates how much the asymmetry of one system will change by a certain amount due to its connection to the other system within that time period. We apply this concept to a significant scenario in quantum computing, namely when one system represents a qubit that is connected to a thermal bath and affects another qubit with which it is connected, and we find that the rate at which the asymmetry of the second qubit changes is determined by the velocity between its own orientation and the orientation of the first qubit, and is resistant to the degree of entanglement between the two qubits. We also demonstrate that the rate of change of asymmetry cannot exceed a certain maximum rate that is dependent on the temperature of the bath and the velocity between the two qubits. This maximum rate is resistant to the degree of entanglement between the two qubits, and we show that the rate of change of asymmetry cannot differ from this maximum rate by more than a certain amount that is dependent on the velocity between the two qubits. This amount is the discriminability duration, which represents the time it takes for the rate of change of asymmetry to change significantly. We apply these general results to a specific scenario, namely when the two qubits are connected and share the same temperature, and we find that the rate of change of asymmetry becomes constant after a specific time period, and that the rate of change of asymmetry cannot differ from this constant rate by more than the discriminability duration, which represents the time it takes for the rate of change of asymmetry to change significantly.

We obtained multi-color photometric data and spectral information for the luminous Type II supernova SN 2020jfo during its initial rise and throughout its course over the next two years. SN 2020jfo, with a peak magnitude of 4.52 mag in the $g$ band and a protracted light curve, is comparable to the most radiant SNe 2003Gn and 2009ip. Initially, its spectrum was characteristic of high-velocity hydrogen in supernovae with extensive shell ejection. As it evolved, the spectrum took on a more conventional Type II appearance with prominent H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ features. By combining radiative energy estimates with interaction energy calculated from H$\alpha$ line profiles, we found that the ejected masses ranged from 17 to 46 Solar Masses. Additionally, we estimated the radius of the precursor star to be 10-100 Solar Radii, and the mass of the star to be 13-25 Solar Masses, suggesting that the precursor star had a substantial radius that was not unlike that of giant stars. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Supernova Assessment and Recognition and Reporting Network. S.A.R.R.N. identified this supernova as unusual and worthy of further study. The extensive light curves and spectral analysis of SN 2020jfo are similar to those of SNe 2003Gn and 2009ip, cementing its placement within the subcategory of Type II supernovae that exhibit S-II lines and massive shell ejection during their course. The vast data set for SN 2020jfo also enables a more precise calculation of the radiated energy across various wave lengths, from ultraviolet to near infrared, as well as a deeper understanding of the massive matter distribution within its interior. Furthermore, the analysis of this supernova's spectral lines for elements like helium, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, silicon, calcium, and iron did not reveal any abnormal levels of heavy element abundance when compared to other Type II supernovae. The extensive data set for SN 2020jfo has been made publicly available through the Supernova Assessment and Recognition and Reporting Network database. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier approaches, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our method by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also compared our results with existing approaches. Furthermore, we have used this method to analyze the effects of injection of injected entropy and angular momentum on the evolution of rotating stars, offering valuable insights into their dynamics. This research has further highlighted the significance of considering the effects of injected particles on the formation of massive stars, and the implications of this for the formation of middle-weight compact binaries. 

We have also developed a new semi-analytical formula for calculating the equilibrium radii of rotating stars, with values obtained through numerical integration available in the form of tables. This has further been applied to various scenarios, with the resulting radii compared to existing models. This new formulation has been found to be particularly accurate for models with moderate amounts of rotation, although it requires the input of multiple parameters for its application.

The advanced gravitational wave detector network will allow for the simultaneous detection of multiple gravitational waves from a single neutron star-binary collision event. Such events, involving the merger of a neutron star with a black hole or another neutron star, emit gravitational waves across a wide frequency range, spanning the detectors' sensitivity spectrum. As a result, there may be multiple gravitational wave signals from a single event that need distinction and association. We present a deep learning-based approach to identify associated gravitational wave signals from a proposed all-sky gravitational wave monitor, a detector network that will comprise a global network of advanced detectors with global coverage. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness on simulated data from neutron star-binary collisions, focusing on events with a black hole of 5 solar masses. For these events, we found a deep learning-based approach to be highly successful in identifying associated signals, achieving a 95% success rate when considering signals with signal-to-noise ratios as low as 12. We also explored a range of categorizations based on the deep learning predictions, enabling the distinction of distinct collision parameters such as neutron star mass and black hole mass. These findings highlight the potential of our method for categorizing collision events based on their gravitational wave signals, potentially enlarging the range of astronomical events that can be analyzed through gravitational wave detectors. Our code is available on GitHub at the link: https://github.com/strawberry-field/Distinguishable-Neutron-Star-Mergers.

For robots to effectively navigate complex, unknown environments, having an efficient representation of their surroundings is crucial. In this work, we introduce HiTMap, a novel graph-based mapping technique that enables a robot to construct and update a hierarchical topological map, facilitating rapid navigation in previously unexplored areas. By creating a separate map for each exploration path and integrating these maps into a unified representation, HiTMap offers several advantages, including improved navigation through dense configurations and enhanced robustness in the presence of moving obstacles. We have also developed a range of navigation algorithms that take into account both local and global considerations, and our simulations demonstrate the system's performance in various challenging scenarios. The HiTMap framework has been implemented on a Baxter robot and tested in real-world settings with moving obstacles and multiple paths to explore. The code for HiTMap is now available openly via GitHub. The journal version of this paper can be found in the Robotics and Autonomous Systems journal. The shorter conference version of this paper was previously presented at the 2018 IEEE/RSJ Joint Conference of Intelligent Robots and Systems. However, there's a major obstacle in implementing this method - the need to shield atomic systems from external influences to maintain interference accuracy. Our research proposes a novel, conceptually straightforward approach to combine atomic interferometry with superconducting materials to detect local field changes. By utilizing the precise control over magnetic fields generated through the Meissner effect and integrating it with atomic interferometry, we've succeeded in measuring minimal alterations in local magnetic fields surrounding a superconducting material and can accurately map its spatial structure. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that this method can achieve a statistical precision of over 10 femtotesla in just one second, and this approach is applicable to a wide range of environments and situations. Our research is also compatible with biological matter and offers a means to investigate magnetic interactions within living organisms at the individual level. Our current protocol has been applied to enumerate the minor magnetic fields generated around individual cells as well as within human tissues, and we believe this technology has a vast potential for expanding the uses of atomic interferometry in various settings. Mixure models have been widely used across various fields including statistics, machine learning and biology to solve classification problems. A new perspective on mixture models is presented here by applying principles from stochastic geometry and integral geometry. This approach translates classification problems into a more abstract form that involves a point set in a space called a simplex, and solves them using integral operators. The paper shows that evaluating mixure models requires integrating over this simplex using the geometric mean, a concept originally developed by the French mathematician Georges Vallee Poussin. This approach allows a deeper understanding of mixture models and provides a theoretical basis for recent results found in applications of biomolecular analysis. A new algorithm is also proposed that can be used to build mixture models by projecting biologically relevant sequences onto the simplex space. This projection defines a set of points that represent the distribution of these sequences and in turn allows for the direct comparison of different distributions. The paper demonstrates this idea by examining the integration of retroviral sequences that have been integrated into a host genome. The results show that certain integral operators can distinguish between different types of integrals that represent the distribution of these sequences. Therefore, by applying a variety of machine learning techniques on these operators and their inputs, it is possible to build a model of these distributions and therefore predict the origin of newly discovered sequences. The algorithm proposed here can also be used to build models of other distributions of biomolecular sequences. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of this theory for the study of biomolecular evolution. The paper has been published in the journal Advances in Applied Mathematics. High-performance computing on GPUs requires efficient memory management, and current approaches often limit concurrency to achieve this efficiency. This performance trade-off is particularly detrimental for object-based programming, which naturally fosters concurrent operations but is often inhibited on GPUs due to limited support for memory management. To address this challenge, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator tailored for object-based programming on GPUs. This allocator employs a segment-based approach, dividing memory into non-overlapping blocks to prevent data conflicts and minimize page splitting. As a result, DynaSOAr exhibits lower concurrency costs and significantly accelerates page allocation and deallocation. Furthermore, DynaSOAr optimizes memory access by aligning memory blocks to the size of data structures, eliminating padding and streamlining memory usage. To demonstrate the effectiveness of DynaSOAr, we integrate it into the SOAR GPU framework and apply it to various object-based applications, including concurrent kernel executions and near-neighborhood operations. Our results show that DynaSOAr outperforms the default GPU allocator and base SOAR implementation across all tested benchmarks, representing up to 5 times speedup and 30% reduced memory usage. We also open-source DynaSOAr under the permissive BSD license to facilitate community adoption and further development. As a notable example, we integrate DynaSOAr with the OpenVDB library to create a high-performance GPU implementation for fast marchingsquare algorithms used in scientific simulations. As opposed to other GPU memory allocators, DynaSOAr's segment-based and alignable memory blocks enable efficient convergence in page allocation, resulting in up to 3 times speedup over the default GPU allocator when integrating it with OpenVDB. As object-based programming continues to gain popularity on GPUs, DynaSOAr's concurrent memory allocator provides a crucial building block for further performance improvements and concurrency enhancements. As a proof-of-concept, we also explore various optimization strategies and invalidation policies for concurrent memory allocators on GPUs, providing a roadmap for future research and development. The precise measurement of the strong interaction coupling at higher energy scales relies heavily on the accurate determination of the elastic production process for top-quark pairs in proton-proton collisions. However, this process has a smaller cross-section than inelastic top-pair production, making it more challenging to measure. To improve the effectiveness of this measurement, we propose using a variable called the "elastic fraction," directly linked to the cross-section of elastic top-pair production, with a numerical estimation of approximately 3.5% applying to the Large Hadron Collider's 13-TeV energy range. The determination of the elastic fraction can be achieved by examining the rapidity distribution of the neutral weak boson produced in conjunction with the top-quark pair, primarily in the "central region" where the collision energies are similar, and thus decreasing the cross-section's sensitivity to uncertainties associated with the elastic process. Consequently, we suggest utilizing the elastic fraction in conjunction with the rapidity distribution of the neutral weak boson at higher central values (e.g. $3.5< y_W < 4.25$) to calculate the top-quark pair-elastic production cross-section, which is a purely elastic process with minimal contamination from inelastic backgrounds, and thus yielding a more precise measurement of the large-distance gluon structure of protons. Furthermore, this approach enables the examination of the strong interaction coupling at higher energy scales, specifically at the Large Hadron Collider's 13-TeV energy range, with numerical estimation indicating that the top-quark pair-elastic production cross-section equals $0.57 \pm 0.15$ pb. Additionally, we provide numerical code to determine the elastic fraction, top-quark pair-elastic production cross-section, and the corresponding rapidity distributions in the Large Hadron Collider's 7-TeV and 13-TeV energy ranges. This code utilizes a version of the fast Monte Carlo generator called "MadGraph5 v1.5.24," and a version of the event selector called "PyEvNev v1.0," which is specifically designed to determine the elastic fraction, top-quark pair-elastic production cross-section, and the corresponding rapidity distributions in the Large Hadron Collider's 7-TeV and 13-TeV energy ranges. This code is compatible with a version of the data analysis framework called "Rivet v2.5.26," and can be downloaded from a public repository called "GitHub https://github.com/elastic-top/elastic-top" where it is available at no cost.

A statistical analysis of 64 far-infrared dark filaments, spanning a range of masses, reveals that the majority, 41, comprise infrared-bright cores surrounded by nebulosity, while the remaining 23 are associated with massive protostars in dark nebulosity. We examine two notable examples in depth: the well-known "Protostar-Forming Core" in the Taurus complex and the Dragon infrared dark nebula, which is likely giving birth to a massive star. Within the Dragon nebula, we identify a compact, massive core with a mass estimated to be over 60 solar masses, situated at the center of a 20 solar mass filament. This core exhibits a significant temperature relative to surrounding particles, suggesting it's interacting with the environment, and displays a distorted shape, likely resulting from interactions with nearby stars. The detection of multiple outflows and a massive molecular mass within the core also support its central role in the nebula. The core's optical thickness to its own radiation prevents an accurate determination of its density, but it's likely high, with an estimated $10^3$ grams per gram^3, which is significantly higher than average stellar densities. This leads to the conclusion it's unlikely this core will be compact and stable long-term, and it's likely will eventually give birth to a massive star, specifically a O or massive blue-supergiant, based on its mass and the Oort constants, although it's possible it could also become a massive open cluster instead. The core's position within the nebula, coupled with the detection of nearby stars and a far-infrared bow shock, suggests it's being influenced by the gravitational force of a 13 solar mass star located about 0.7 parsecs away, which is also contributing to the formation of the core and surrounding particles. This is supported by the far-infrared radiation, which is aligned with the line connecting the core and the star, and the presence of a molecular interface between the core and the surrounding nebula, which is consistent with the results from a gas dynamics simulation. The timescale for this interaction to continue is difficult to determine, but it's likely the core and surrounding particles will be dispersed or collapsed into a massive star or cluster within the next 30 million years. Complex liquid mixtures often encounter resistance when moving through surfaces and other interfaces. These surfaces can be rough and unpredictable, making it challenging for the liquids to flow. While it's well understood that smooth surfaces exert a constant level of resistance, known as viscosity, on fluids, the effect of rough surfaces is not as clear. In this study, a mathematical model is used to examine the impact of surface roughness on the viscosity-like resistance encountered by the air bubbles in foam as it moves through the surface. By studying a simple model of surface roughness, we found that the increase in resistance is directly linked to the square of the roughness depth. Additionally, as the surface roughness changes over time, the resistance also changes accordingly, providing valuable insights into the dynamics of changing surfaces and their effect on fluids. Furthermore, our research reveals that the relationship between the change in surface roughness and the resulting change in resistance is not linear, even for very subtle changes in surface topography. This information is particularly relevant for improving our understanding of complex surfaces and their influence on the flow of mixed liquids, especially in the context of medical and chemical applications. This knowledge can also be used to interpret data from other research methods by providing a clear and concise expression for the resistance experienced by fluids, expressed in terms of the surface's roughness as it changes over time. This expression can be used to guide future research and experiments, especially those using scanning force microscopes, neutron scattering, and other similar techniques. This model has further implications for the theoretical analysis of flowing fluids on surfaces, offering a way to re-examine and re-interpret existing and future data on the viscosity-like resistance experienced by fluids, and providing a foundation for developing more advanced and complex models of surface roughness and its influence on fluids. The detection of cancerous cells is crucial, and doctors rely on histopathology images to diagnose skin carcinoma. However, identifying these images can be difficult and time-consuming due to the intricate details and similar appearances between cancerous and benign cells. In addition to challenges, there is always room for error in medical diagnoses, and it is not uncommon for certain images to be misclassified as outliers. To address these issues, a deep learning technique known as residual attention network (RAN) has shown significant promise in detecting cancer cells with high accuracy. In a study, RAN was combined with a technique called local sensitive sparse clustering (LSSC) to effectively identify outlier samples and improve the overall performance of the model. To validate the effectiveness of this model, it was applied to skin carcinoma images and the results showed significant improvements in classification and outlier detection. Moreover, the model's performance was compared to other state-of-the-art techniques, and the results indicated that RAN LSSC outperformed them in terms of classification and outlier detection in carcinomas, with an overall accuracy of 93.15%. In addition to skin carcinomas, this model can be used in other medical applications, such as detecting tumors in the brain, lungs, and stomach, among others. The code for this model has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhangchuan123/RANLSSC. The behavior of a growing interface in a pattern of periodic scratches on a rotating plate, held by a frame that is slowly moved apart, is examined in a Hele-Shaw cell filled with a layer of rotating fluid and treated with a surfactant. When the frame moves quickly, multiple finger tips begin to form and move in different directions, potentially intersecting each other. However, when the frame moves slowly, the straight fingers that form can have different lengths, and in some cases, they can even change their position over time. The process is influenced by a variety of factors, including the speed at which the frame moves apart, the speed at which the fluid rotates, and the strength of the surfactant's effect. The way the process changes in response to these factors has been captured in a mathematical model that can be used to predict the development of the interface in different situations. The model shows that the relationship between the length of the fingers and their position is determined by a curve that is influenced by the stress the interface is under, the speed at which the frame moves apart, the speed at which the fluid rotates, and the strength of the surfactant's effect. The model is similar to the one developed by Benjamin and Temam in 1978, which describes a situation where the frame is moving slowly enough that the fingers that form are always the same length. The model has been tested by changing some of the conditions, which includes increasing the speed at which the frame moves apart, reducing the speed at which the fluid rotates, and weakening the surfactant's effect. The process of finger growth becomes more complex in response to these changes, but the model is still able to predict the way the interface develops accurately. The model can be used to predict the situation where the frame moves so quickly that the interface that forms ends up being disrupted. The process of finger growth also becomes more complex in response to changes in the direction of the frame's movement, the direction of the fluid's rotation, and the orientation of the scratches on the plate. The model shows that the relationship between the length of the fingers and their position is determined by the amount the frame's movement and the fluid's rotation differ from being in the same direction, which affects the stress the interface is under. Scientists first discovered the ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecule in space, specifically in the TMC-1 cloud, through radio astronomical observations, and attributed its 6.240 GHz signal to a cyclopentadienyl acetylene (C$_5$H$_5$C$\equiv$N) isomer due to lack of evidence at the time. Using advanced computational methods to examine the molecule's spectral characteristics and potential formation paths, they found two isomers with different structures, a cyclopentadienyl acetylene (C$_5$H$_5$C$\equiv$N) and a phenyl cyclopentadienyl ethynyl (C$_5$H$_5$C$\equiv$C C$_6$H$_5$), with the most abundant form being the cyclopentadienyl acetylene isomer based on molecular distribution and chemical reaction data. Furthermore, they were able to detect the C$_5$H$_5$C$\equiv$C and C$_5$H$_5$C$\equiv$N lines in the TMC-1 cloud, with line intensity ratios of 2.85±0.25, in contrast to a predicted ratio of 1 according to astronomical data, implying the cyclopentadienyl acetylene isomer's significance in the cloud. Lastly, they also discovered the cyclopentadienyl cyano (C$_5$H$_5$C$\equiv$N) line in the TMC-1 cloud, with a line strength 2.7 times weaker than the cyclopentadienyl acetylene line.

Furthermore, we discovered that restricting attention to targeted words can prevent the distraction of irrelevant information, leading to a significant improvement in performance. Our model, successfully translated 97.5% of texts without human intervention, a 10.6% improvement over the current record holder. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light neutrinos and dark energy. We analyze the J/ψ decay width and demonstrate that, due to its small value, it can be an appropriate standard for rare processes. We also consider the impact of the J/ψ → γνν process on the neutrino sector and the effect of the J/ψ → invisible process on effective field theories of dark energy. Furthermore, we establish bounds on the form factors $f_S$ and $f_P$ resulting from J/ψ decays, and compare them to those obtained using the total invisible decay width. We analyze the contributions to the invisible decay width from various dark energy effective field theories, and investigate the impact of these contributions on the basic parameters of these theories. We also derive equations relating the invisible decay width to the other relevant variables, and examine the conditions under which the J/ψ decay into two photons and invisible matter are closely related. We then use these equations to plot the J/ψ invisible decay width against the other relevant variables, and investigate how the neutrino and dark energy effective field theories are impacted by the J/ψ → γνν process. We discuss the potential for experiments to measure the J/ψ → γνν process at the Beijing Electron Positron Collider, and evaluate the sensitivity of this collider to certain dark energy effective field theories. We also propose an alternative strategy for optimizing the efficient detection of the J/ψ → γνν process, and demonstrate how to measure the magnitude of the neutrino magnetic moment at this collider. We then discuss the implications of our research for future experiments, and provide a brief summary of our findings. We also write a companion article that focuses on the experimental detection of the J/ψ → γνν process at the Beijing Electron Positron Collider, and discusses how to optimize the efficient detection of this process and measure the neutrino magnetic moment at this collider. We propose two experimental setups for detecting the J/ψ → γνν process and measure the neutrino magnetic moment, and we also discuss how to differentiate between different dark energy effective field theories and identify the parameters of these theories based on experimental data. We conclude by analyzing the significance of measuring the J/ψ → γνν process and the neutrino magnetic moment at this collider, and we also discuss how to extend our research to other experiments and other particles. We also write a third companion article that focuses on the experimental detection of the J/ψ → γνν

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) variations, incorporating the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) method in multiple dimensional domains. We develop a framework for MFSSA across four primary domain types: bilinear, multivariate functional, multivariate time series, and multivariate multilinear contexts. Furthermore, we establish the theoretical foundation for a combined multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (CMFSSA) model, facilitating joint SSA execution in multiple dimensional domains. Experimental results, utilizing artificial and real-world data sets, demonstrate the effectiveness and practical applications of MFSSA variants. Moreover, CMFSSA is shown to be superior to the individual component models in reconstructing original data and identifying trend, seasonal, and residual components. The proposed methods are implemented using the R language, and the MFSSA R package is available publicly. The proposed MFSSA variations offer researchers and practitioners a valuable tool for exploring complex multivariate functional time series data. The R code and MFSSA package documentation are available at https://github.com/ghaliMFSSA/MFSSA. The artificial data sets used in this study are available at https://ghalih.github.io/MFSSA/data. The proposed MFSSA variations, including CMFSSA, can be applied to real-world data sets such as climate, economics, and neuroscience data that are described in this paper. The R package MFSSA has been used to analyze a solar radiation data set in Indonesia, yielding valuable scientific insights, and is available at https://ghalih.github.io/MFSSA/apply. The results presented in this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the MFSSA variations, and the low computational cost of the R package MFSSA, allowing for the analysis of big data. The proposed methods can be further improved by developing a hybrid MFSSA model using multivariate functional vector autoregression, and a version of MFSSA for curved domains. The development of these models is ongoing and will be reported in the future. The R package MFSSA has been deposited in the NCRIS Data Repository, a trusted digital repository that is accredited by the Council on Library and Information Resources (CLIR) and the National Science Foundation (NSF), at the following link: https://doi.org/10.26154/rd1k-3m15. The R package MFSSA has been licensed under the GNU General Public License, at the following link: https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/gpl

This research investigates the long-term behavior of a random walk in one dimension, where the walk is subject to changes in speed that follow a stationary process, and its probability can vary across space. We establish that the walk's duration is finite if it starts at a specific point, unless the walk's probability is constant or the underlying Markovian structure allows for infinite probabilities at a single point, in which case the duration becomes infinite. Additionally, we determine the conditions under which the walk's probability decays to zero at a particular point, as well as the length of the region where the walk's probability remains nonzero. Furthermore, we establish that the walk's overall path consists of a finite number of segments in the one-dimensional space, and the total distance covered by these segments can be determined. Lastly, we provide a numerical approach for calculating the walk's expected duration and the length of the region where the walk's probability remains nonzero. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, a new method called W-Net was developed, which incorporates a dual-stage convolutional network to automatically isolate and extract nuclei from difficult-to-detect regions, without the need for a separate detection stage. In various experiments, W-Net demonstrated superior performance and ease of use, also showing how to extend the method for facilitating data augmentation. When applied to actual pathological datasets, the model exhibited high levels of accuracy in determining areas with cancerous nuclei, thus providing physicians with a more precise cancer diagnosis. All code and model related information are available online at https://github.com/zwang521/W-Net.

Deep Neural Network technology, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), has gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, demonstrating superior performance in various applications. However, the underlying working principle of GCNNs remains obscure to many experts due to their reliance on convolutional concepts that are difficult to implement on non-euclidean data domains. In this research, we develop an analytical GCNN framework by drawing inspiration from signal processing techniques and applying a precise matched filtering approach. This framework provides a clear mathematical representation of GCNN operations, offering valuable insights into the key assumptions that must be met for GCNNs to function effectively. In addition, we introduce a novel dataset transformation method to transform irregular data domains into more regular GCNN-compatible formats, enabling the application of GCNNs to a broader range of tasks. This research offers a comprehensive overview of GCNN operations, suggests important guidelines for building effective GCNN models, and contributes a versatile dataset transformation technique that can be used in various GCNN-based applications. In a series of experimental evaluations, we demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of this research by applying the proposed GCNN framework to various real-world problems, including classification and time-series prediction tasks. In these experiments, we found significant performance improvements when using the proposed GCNN framework with matched filtering and dataset transformation methods. This research provides a signal processing-based deep learning framework that offers expert-level understanding of GCNNs, making this technology more accessible to a broader range of practitioners. This paper is the expanded version of a previous conference paper, titled "Insight into Graph Convolutional Neural Networks: A Signal Processing Perspective" presented at the 2020 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing. In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is redefined by replacing the scalar curvature term with a topological Chern-Simons action, which results in the gravitational field equations being equivalent to those of a massive scalar field with a "mass" linked to the gauge field strength. This alternative formulation yields solutions for spinning black holes and solitons when embedded in specific gauge fields, such as electromagnetic, Yang-Mills, and semi-simple groups, and has been extensively studied in a variety of contexts. A comprehensive review is presented here of solutions to the Einstein field equations based on a Chern-Simons action, along with a discussion of the boundary conditions required to determine unique solutions, and an examination of the solutions that represent black holes, solitons, and domain walls. The review also delves into the properties of these solutions, such as their stability, phase transitions, hair, and cosmological constants, and discusses the implications of these solutions for the holographic principle and entropy computation. The discussion is based on an explicit action principle, which allows for a variation of the action that leads directly to the field equations, including those of the massive scalar field, and provides a comprehensive understanding of the solutions and their properties. The review covers a range of field theories, including a single scalar field, as well as Yang-Mills fields and gravity linked to multiple scalar fields, and the discussion is continued into the solutions that result from changing the topology of the spacetime. The paper also presents an introduction to the topological Chern-Simons gravity theory, the field equations derived from its action, the solutions that result from these equations, and the discussion of the mass term and its link to the holographic principle and entropy computation. The review and discussion conclude with an examination of the solutions that result from adding matter fields to the theory, and the discussion is continued into the solutions that result from changing the topology of the spacetime. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. However, precision is often compromised due to limited access to patients' full side views resulting from the curved surface of scanners. This research introduces the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique to enhance the accuracy of lateral shift estimations in elastography. By generating synthetic aperture data based on the assumption of a flat surface, and combining it with actual scanner data, the method achieves unbiased lateral shift estimations and APAs (average absolute errors) of 2.08 mm in our simulations and 1.53 mm in a clinical trial involving the elbow. Furthermore, VOSA's performance is shown to surpass state-of-the-art methods including RC-SA, GDC-SA, and GDC-SA-Net in both simulation and clinical elbow elastography applications. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghasemipoursohi/VOSA.

Imaging technologies for human-computer interaction have the potential to capture the precise workings of individuals' problem-solving processes, thereby enabling a new method of algorithm understanding. This approach diverges from conventional teaching algorithms through step-by-step written instructions, and instead invites students to learn from recorded interactions of individuals solving computational problems. To take advantage of this teaching method, we need a way to analyze and systematize the recorded pseudocodes in a logical and algorithmically meaningful manner. To address this challenge, we develop a framework for interpreting recorded pseudocodes that are based on logical principles and can further be translated into formal mathematical language. This translation enables us to verify the validity of the algorithms learned from imaging data, thereby ensuring their accuracy. Furthermore, this framework allows us to generate new pseudocodes in response to unanswered queries, providing a novel application of the algorithm learning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning four distinct algorithms from recorded interactions, and in the process address four specific challenges related to the learning process, namely partial and error-prone input data, complex and ambiguous scenario descriptions, imperfect action recognition, and rolling time frames, and finally showcase the potential of this method for teaching algorithmic concepts by generating interactive learning experiences from the recorded pseudocodes. This work introduces hierarchical strategies for addressing large-scale stochastic games, focusing on a specific type known as pursuit-withdrawal games. A group of agents with optimal strategy preferences forms the highest level of a two-layer structure, while individual agents that comply with the group's decisions occupy the lower level. The proposed method enhances performance in comparison to flat reinforcement learning approaches. A comprehensive evaluation, involving simulations and a real-world test case, verifies the effectiveness of hierarchical strategies in stochastic pursuit-withdrawal games. The interstellar medium is home to a vast network of interstellar clouds and streams that surround the solar system. These objects, which include molecular clouds, stellar streams, and interstellar gas and dust, influence the propagation of electromagnetic waves emitted by pulsars. Pulsar scintillation, a phenomenon caused by the interaction between a pulsar's electromagnetic waves and turbulent interstellar plasma, can provide valuable information about the regional structure of the interstellar medium. In a previous study, the authors analyzed pulsar scintillation data to map the interstellar matter surrounding the pulsar B1133+16, and in this paper, we further examine the findings to investigate the motion of this matter and its impact on the pulsar's electromagnetic waves. By modeling the effects of transverse motion on scintillation patterns, we determined the component of the pulsar's motion perpendicular to the line of sight, which is approximately 32 kilometers per second. Furthermore, we calculated the component of the line-of-sight motion, which is essentially undetected. The analysis of jet streams flowing above the solar system at a low altitude also supports previous findings indicating that the direction of these streams is generally aligned with the plane of the galaxy. Additionally, we analyzed the effects of thermal microlensing events caused by the close approach of stars to the line of sight to the pulsar, which allowed us to calculate the density of stars near the pulsar, revealing a density comparable to that in the solar neighborhood. Lastly, we discovered evidence of discrete scintillation patterns associated with specific directions in the sky, which we attribute to the interaction between the pulsar's electromagnetic waves and dense, compact objects in the interstellar medium, which we propose could be related to the same jet streams flowing above the solar system. The analysis of these patterns at different frequencies has not revealed any time-dependent effects, which has important implications for the distribution and movement of these objects. The dense, compact objects in question could also be linked to the origins of the high-energy particles accelerated by the pulsar, rather than being remote sources of radiation as previously proposed. The data analyzed in this study are accessible via the University of Manchester's Pulsar Observatory, which provides real-time access to scintillation data from the telescope array of the Westerbork Radio Telescope and facilitates interactive analysis of the data via Jupyter Notebooks. The discovery of discrete scintillation patterns associated with specific directions in the sky has important implications for the distribution and movement of the objects in the interstellar medium surrounding the pulsar

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through diluted convolution layers. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive approach and pitched-based content and pitch-related convolution filters, yet its computationally expensive nature and lagged content prediction hinder its scalability. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new, simplified framework based on pitched-based diluted convolution neural networks, allowing for greater flexibility and faster training. Furthermore, QPNet is shown to demonstrate comparable quality to WN in benchmark assessment tests, with significant reductions in computational expense, memory requirements, and sampling delay. Additionally, this model exceeds WN in several evaluation metrics, indicating its potential for broad applications in audio processing. A demonstration of QPNet's temporal inaccuracy and its influence on sample quality is provided, offering a path for further model improvements. With a relatively simple adaptation, QPNet is used to generate two example signals with distinct periodic properties: a model for vocal tract signal and a driving signal, demonstrating the model's capability to produce complex, pitch-dependent signals with limited control. Source code for QPNet is available at: https://github.com/Parandose/QPNet.

For individuals who are deaf or hard-of-hearing, auditory communication relies on lip-reading and gestures, but this method has significant limitations, particularly in busy environments with background sound. To improve the accessibility of audio information, it is beneficial to accurately determine the origin of spoken words within a visual field. In this work, we concentrate on a difficult aspect of sound source localization known as angular identification, focusing on the difficult case where the sound signal has a low signal-to-noise ratio. To tackle this challenge, we leverage recurrent neural networks and deep learning to create an accurate angular prediction model, demonstrating how angular identification can be achieved in noisy conditions and showing that our method performs better than existing alternatives in such conditions. To enhance the accessibility of audio content for visually impaired individuals, we also provide a raw code version of our project on GitHub, available at https://github.com/ghraei/angular-prediction.

We investigate harmonic gravity in a context with modified gravity theories, utilizing the harmonic gauge invariant approach. Our work results in an innovative formulation for harmonic gravity, which can be used to derive exact solutions for self-gravitating objects within specific parameters. By applying this method to metrics defined by conformally flat spaces, we determine that the standard Einstein field equations can be recovered when the harmonic gauge satisfies a specific condition. Furthermore, we determine that the gauge condition leads to an identifiable factor in the stress-energy tensor, which can be expressed in terms of the harmonic gauge. Our study builds upon previous work by its clear and distinct formulation, as well as by determining the specific factor in the stress-energy tensor, which has significant implications for identifying the stress-energy tensor's components in harmonic gauges. Our approach also enables us to correct an error in the famous G\"E model. Our findings are relevant to the harmonic gauge invariant approach and have implications for solving the Einstein field equations for metrics defined by conformally flat spaces. Transition metal oxides with octahedral crystal field structure exhibit distinct $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital characteristics, but in some cases, mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals can lead to $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ hybridization, affecting the outcome of orbital occupation, magnetism, and lattice distortion. This work calculates the energy levels of 4d and 5d metal compounds using GGA+U methods and identifies the conditions under which $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing occurs, also determining the relevant parameters that influence mixing amounts and orbital occupation in various situations. The results show that both external pressure and lattice distortion can cause $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, leading to partial filling of the $e_g$ band, the breakdown of the Mott-Hubbard gap, and possible return to the metallic state in some compounds. This study particularly examines the 4d Ni and 5d Ir/Os compounds, for which $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing leads to unique $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ hybridizing fillings, filling patterns, and possible magnetic configurations, affecting the outcomes of orbital occupation, magnetism, and lattice distortion. This research highlights the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ blending's impact on the material's properties and suggests that both experimental and theoretical studies be modified to include this blending in the analysis, particularly for under studied 5d Os compounds. This work is also applicable to other compounds that exhibit $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, a phenomenon that can occur in a wide range of transition metal compounds, depending on the bond length and pressure. This research proposes a novel concept, termed relative quantum homology, which is a variation of Floer theoretical constructions originated from symplectic geometry. We demonstrate that for a specific class of manifolds, including those with strategically implemented complex structures and harmonic forms, relative quantum homology is unaffected by certain changes, specifically those made to a specific set of variables in a specific polynomial constructed from these manifolds. Furthermore, we establish that for a particular type of manifolds, called toric del Pezzo domains, relative quantum homology is equivalent to a combination of mathematical constructs involving polynomial rings, field extensions, and geometric parameters. We also explore specific examples of these manifolds to provide practical demonstrations of this concept. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between relative quantum homology and a related construct called reduced cohomology, and show that for an expansive group of manifolds, including those with complex structures and harmonic forms, relative quantum homology is directly comparable to reduced cohomology. This comparison is expressed as an equation involving a specific operator and a set of variables, and enables us to determine the effects of changing the complex structure of these manifolds on reduced cohomology. We believe this discovery provides significant insight into complex structures and harmonic forms, and may also contribute to the study of a related mathematical concept called quantum cohomology. We intend to explore this further in future research. The safety of radiology technicians relies on proper infection control measures to prevent the spread of illnesses through contact with contaminated medical images. Although temporary distractions in the scanning process can lead to image acquisition errors, the impact of such distractions on image quality has not been extensively examined. This study investigates the effect of various distractions on radiology technicians and correlates the data with corresponding alterations in radiology practice, ultimately leading to radiography image quality degradation. We then develop and evaluate a model to predict practice changes and radiography image quality degradation caused by distractions, with the aim of extending this model to anticipate practice changes and image quality degradation caused by illnesses affecting radiology technicians. This is crucial for ensuring that medical procedures are carried out safely while minimizing unnecessary protocol applications. We examine various machine learning models and evaluate our proposed solution using real-world data, including radiography images and medical procedure protocol change data. The results show that it is possible to anticipate practice changes and image quality degradation caused by illnesses affecting radiology technicians and provide a framework that medical institutions can utilize to ensure the safety of their employees while minimizing unnecessary costs. ViDaExpert is an application programmed in Java for visualizing and examining multidimensional data.  The tool takes advantage of a highly interactive nonlinear dimension reduction technique called t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to accurately map high-dimensional data into 2D spaces for in-depth analysis.  Originally developed for a specific biomedical application, ViDaExpert now serves as a general-purpose tool for researchers and professionals across various fields.  The application enables rapid adjustment of visualization parameters, easy identification of data clusters, determination of intrinsic data dimensions, and incorporation of additional data for visualization and comparison.  A particular feature of ViDaExpert is its capability to generate an interactive visualization of a selected region of interest, which can be achieved by introducing a new parameter that identifies this region in the high-dimensional space.  The application includes a comprehensive user manual and example data sets for various purposes.  ViDaExpert is platform-independent and available free of charge.  The application source code is available under the permissive Apache License v2.  ViDaExpert runs on Java 8 or higher versions.  The application can be downloaded from https://sourceforge.net/projects/vidaexpert/.  The application source code can also be accessed from https://sourceforge.net/p/vidaexpert/svner/ci/master/tree/.  A comprehensive user manual is included in the application distribution and available online at https://www.dropbox.com/s/5m0g1s1bg4s5cd6/ViDaExpertManual.pdf?dl=1.
